title: The Compass of the Cape Route
premise: In 1898, Noor Montrose, a pearl diver's son indentured to the Cape Route Trading Company, has spent his life erasing himself from ledgers and memories alike. When a census taker's probing questions expose his family's false identities, colonial authorities begin compiling lists for 'repatriation' aboard a ship with too few berths. As Noor uses his insider access to forge documents, he must decide which of his family members gets the last berth—his fading mother, who remembers a homeland he's never seen, or his younger sister, who carries their future. In the end, Noor gives up his own place, staying behind to keep the truth alive in the company's records, discovering that identity is not what is written about you but what you choose to carry.
about_author: Gideon Yarrow is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing colonial shipping manifests before turning to fiction. His novels explore the quiet violence of paperwork and the people history tried not to count.

chapters.title: The Weight of Water
chapters.summary: Noor dives for pearls at dawn while reciting the false family name the trading company assigned them. POV: Noor. The emotional beat is quiet endurance—he measures everything by what can be carried, establishing his survival philosophy and the family's fragile invisibility.

chapters.title: A Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Census taker Elias Brand arrives at the company compound, polite and relentless, asking where Noor's mother was born. POV: Noor. The beat is dread blooming into realization: their invented past has a seam, and Brand found it.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Lies
chapters.summary: Noor searches the company archives at night, discovering decades of altered records—and that others before him were erased entirely. POV: Noor. The emotional beat shifts from fear to fury as he understands invisibility was always someone else's decision.

chapters.title: Mother's Salt Garden
chapters.summary: His mother, memory failing, mistakes Noor for his dead father and describes a homeland across the sea in vivid detail. POV: alternating Noor and mother. The beat is tender heartbreak: her memories are the only true inheritance left.

chapters.title: The Repatriation List
chapters.summary: Brand returns with official orders: families with irregular papers will be listed for transport on the Meridian Star, which has exactly one berth fewer than needed. POV: Noor. The beat is cold panic—the abstraction becomes arithmetic, and the arithmetic is his family.

chapters.title: What the Sister Carries
chapters.summary: Noor's sister Amara reveals she has been secretly teaching herself letters using discarded manifests, dreaming of a life beyond the cape. POV: Amara. The beat is defiant hope that complicates Noor's calculus: she is not cargo but a future.

chapters.title: Forged in Ink
chapters.summary: Noor forges documents to create an extra berth, enlisting a sympathetic clerk whose price is dangerous: testimony against the company director. POV: Noor. The beat is moral vertigo—loyalty to family now demands betrayal of the institution that owns him.

chapters.title: The Director's Table
chapters.summary: The director confronts Noor, offering him freedom and status if he names other families hiding irregular papers. POV: Noor. The climax of temptation: truth as currency, loyalty as leverage. He refuses, knowing the cost.

chapters.title: Last Berth
chapters.summary: At the dock, chaos erupts as the list is read aloud; Noor must choose in minutes between his mother and Amara. POV: Noor. The emotional climax: he puts Amara aboard, and his mother, lucid for one moment, presses her homeland's memory into his hands like a compass.

chapters.title: The Man Who Stayed Counted
chapters.summary: Noor remains, testifying before a commission, his name finally written plainly in the record. POV: Noor, years later. The resolution is bittersweet peace: Amara's letters arrive from abroad, and Noor learns that being seen—even at terrible cost—was the only way to be real.
